title: Introduction to Python & Features
partA_intro: Python is a popular, high-level, interpreted programming language created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991. It is designed to be extremely easy to read, write, and learn, making it the ideal first language for students with zero coding background.
partB_realLife: Think of English as a language we speak every day. Traditional programming languages like C or C++ are like legal court documents with complex rules and punctuation everywhere. Python is like speaking plain, simple English with a friend—concise, clear, and direct.
partC_hinglish: Agar aapne pehle kabhi programming nahi seekhi hai, toh tension lene ki bilkul zaroorat nahi hai! Python ko aise banaya gaya hai ki iska code lagbhag aam English jaisa lagta hai. C ya Java mein jo kaam 10 lines mein hota hai, Python mein wahi kaam sirf 1 ya 2 lines mein ho jata hai. Isko sikhna aur exam mein likhna dono bahut aasan hai.
partD_examDef: Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically-typed, and general-purpose programming language that emphasizes code readability with its notable use of significant whitespace/indentation.
partE_points: Easy to Learn & Read: Syntax is clean, simple, and resembles plain English.
Interpreted Language: Python code is executed line-by-line, which makes debugging and finding errors easy.
Dynamically Typed: You do NOT need to declare data types (e.g., int, float) before using a variable; Python detects it automatically.
Platform Independent / Portable: Write once, run on Windows, Mac, Linux, or Android without code changes.
Free and Open Source: Free to use and distribute.
partF_syntax:
# Simple Python Output Syntax
print("Your message here")
partG_example:
# Program to display a welcome message for college exam
print("Welcome to Python Programming")
print("Course: BSC/BA/CSE/MD/5/DSC/301")
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: # Program... is a comment, Python ignores it completely.
Line 2: print("Welcome...") outputs the greeting text to the user's screen.
Line 3: print("Course...") outputs the exact course code on the next line.
partJ_output:
Welcome to Python Programming
Course: BSC/BA/CSE/MD/5/DSC/301
partK_mistakes: Writing 'Print' instead of 'print'. Python is strictly case-sensitive; function names are lowercase.
Forgetting double or single quotes around text inside print(). e.g., print(Hello) will cause NameError.

oneMark.q: Who developed Python and in which year?
Is Python a compiled or interpreted language?
oneMark.a: Python is an interpreted language (code executes line-by-line).

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Mention four salient features of Python.
Ans: 1. Easy to learn and read, 2. Interpreted nature, 3. Dynamically typed, 4. Free and platform-independent.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Explain the history, features, and advantages of Python in detail with suitable examples.

partM_revision: Python was created by Guido van Rossum (1991). Key features: Interpreted, High-level, Dynamically typed, Simple English-like syntax, Case-sensitive.

title: Keywords & Identifiers (Naming Rules)
partA_intro: Keywords are special words already booked by Python for internal commands. Identifiers are custom names given by the programmer to variables, functions, and lists.
partB_realLife: Consider traffic rules. Words like 'STOP' and 'ONE-WAY' have fixed meanings for drivers (Keywords). But your own name, roll number, or locker number are custom labels you choose (Identifiers). You cannot name a child 'STOP' in a traffic book!
partC_hinglish: Keywords wo words hain jo Python ne apne system ke liye pehle se reserve kar rakhe hain (jaise if, else, while, for). Aap inka naam kisi variable ya program ko nahi de sakte. Identifiers wo naam hain jo aap khud decide karte hain (jaise student_name, age, marks). Identifiers rakhne ke kuch pakke rules hote hain jo exam mein har saal aate hain.
partD_examDef: Keywords are reserved words in Python with predefined syntactic meanings that cannot be used as identifiers. Identifiers are user-defined names given to variables, functions, or classes to uniquely identify them in memory.
partE_points: Total Keywords: Around 35 keywords in Python 3 (e.g., if, elif, else, while, for, in, is, def, return, True, False, None).
Golden Exam Fact: All keywords are lowercase EXCEPT THREE: True, False, None.
Rule 1 for Identifiers: Can contain letters (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9), and underscore (_).
Rule 2 for Identifiers: MUST start with a letter or underscore (_). CAN NEVER start with a digit! (e.g., 1st_rank is ILLEGAL).
Rule 3 for Identifiers: Special characters (@, $, %, -, spaces) are strictly PROHIBITED.
Rule 4 for Identifiers: Keywords cannot be used as identifiers.
partF_syntax:
# Valid Identifiers:
age = 20
_total_marks = 85
student1 = "Priya"

# Invalid Identifiers:
# 1student = "Priya"  (Error: Starts with digit)
# total marks = 85    (Error: Contains space)
# class = 5           (Error: 'class' is a keyword)
partG_example:
# Demonstration of Valid Identifiers
roll_no = 101
student_name = "Anjali"
_marks_sem5 = 32.5

print("Roll Number:", roll_no)
print("Student Name:", student_name)
print("Marks:", _marks_sem5)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: roll_no is a valid identifier using letters and underscore.
Line 2: student_name stores string value "Anjali".
Line 3: _marks_sem5 starts with an underscore, which is completely valid.
Lines 4-6: print() displays the labels and variable contents.
partJ_output:
Roll Number: 101
Student Name: Anjali
Marks: 32.5
partK_mistakes: Starting identifier with a number: e.g., 2nd_num = 50 gives SyntaxError.
Using hyphens instead of underscores: roll-no gives SyntaxError because '-' is treated as subtraction operator.
Confusing True/False capitalization: writing true = 5 (lowercase is technically allowed as identifier, but highly discouraged and confusing; True is the keyword).

oneMark.q: Which 3 Python keywords start with a capital letter?
Is '2var' a valid identifier in Python? Give reason.
oneMark.a: No, because identifiers cannot begin with a numeric digit.

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: State the 4 rules for naming identifiers in Python.
Ans: 1. Can contain a-z, A-Z, 0-9, and _. 2. Must begin with a letter or underscore. 3. Cannot contain spaces or special symbols. 4. Cannot be a reserved keyword.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What are keywords and identifiers? Explain the rules for naming identifiers with valid and invalid examples.

partM_revision: Keywords = Python's reserved words (if, for, True). Identifiers = User's custom variable/function names. Never start an identifier with a digit or include spaces!

title: Comments (#) vs Docstrings (Triple Quotes)
partA_intro: Comments are non-executable explanatory notes written inside the program code for human readers. In Python, '#' is the official syntax for single-line comments. Python does NOT have a dedicated multiline comment syntax. Triple-quoted strings (''' or """) are technically string literals, but when not assigned to any variable, they are ignored by Python or used as docstrings to document functions and modules.
partB_realLife: Think of a sticky note pasted on a textbook page. When the teacher reads the main book, your sticky note is just for your own memory and understanding; it is not part of the exam question paper.
partC_hinglish: Comments wo notes hote hain jo hum apne ya doosre programmers ke samajhne ke liye likhte hain. Python in lines ko bilkul ignore (skip) kar deta hai. Python mein single-line comment ke liye '#' use hota hai. Ek bahut important technical baat jo viva aur exam mein aati hai: Python mein multiline comment ke liye koi alag keyword ya syntax nahi hota! Hum multiple lines par '#' laga sakte hain, ya phir triple quotes (''' ya """) use karte hain. Triple quotes asal mein string literals hote hain; agar unhe kisi variable ko na dein toh Python unhe execute nahi karta, aur jab wo kisi function/class ke top par hote hain toh unhe 'Docstrings' kaha jata hai.
partD_examDef: Comments are non-executable text statements in Python source code marked with '#' used for program documentation. Python has no native multi-line comment token; instead, consecutive '#' characters or unassigned triple-quoted string literals (often utilized as docstrings) serve multi-line explanatory purposes.
partE_points: Single-line Comment: Uses the hash symbol (#). Everything from # to the end of that line is ignored by the interpreter.
Inline Comment: A comment placed at the end of an executable statement (e.g., x = 10 # storing age).
No Native Multiline Comment Syntax: Python does NOT possess a /* ... */ construct like C/Java.
Multiline Comment convention: Created either by placing '#' at the beginning of each line, or using triple-quoted string blocks (''' or """).

Docstrings vs Comments: Triple-quoted strings placed right at the beginning of a function, class, or module are 'docstrings'. Unlike comments, docstrings are retained at runtime in the __doc__ attribute.
partF_syntax:
# Single line comment
# Line 1 of multiline comment
# Line 2 of multiline comment

"""
Triple-quoted string literal used as
a multiline documentation block / docstring.
"""
partG_example:
# Program to demonstrate single-line comments and docstrings

# Initializing student marks
marks = 45  # Pass marks threshold is 35

"""
This multiline block is an unassigned string literal.
Because it is unassigned, Python skips it during execution.
"""
print('Final Student Marks:', marks)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: # Program... Python sees '#' and ignores the entire line.
Line 3: # Initializing... Comment line ignored by interpreter.
Line 4: marks = 45 is executed; '# Pass marks...' at the line end is ignored as an inline comment.
Lines 6-9: Triple quotes enclose a multiline string literal; since it is not assigned to any variable, it is evaluated and discarded (acting as a comment block).
Line 10: print() outputs the string and variable value.
partJ_output: Final Student Marks: 45
partK_mistakes: Using // for comments. // is single-line comment in C/C++/Java, but in Python // is the floor division operator!
Using /* ... */ for comments. Python does not support C-style block comments.

oneMark.q: Which symbol is used for single-line comments in Python?
Does Python execute comments during program runtime?
oneMark.a: No, comments are non-executable and ignored by the interpreter.

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: What is the difference between a comment and a docstring in Python?
Ans: Comments start with '#' and are completely stripped during compilation. Docstrings are triple-quoted string literals placed at the start of modules/functions, which are stored in the object's __doc__ attribute and accessible at runtime.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What are comments? Explain their purpose, types (single-line and multiline) with syntax and practical Python examples.

partM_revision: Single line comment = '#'. Python has NO native multiline comment symbol. Triple quotes ('''/""") are string literals used as docstrings/multiline notes.

title: Variables: Declaration, Assignment, Reading Input & Naming Restrictions
partA_intro: A variable is a named storage location in computer memory that holds data. When you want to store a number, name, or score in your program so that you can use it later, you store it in a variable.
partB_realLife: Think of labelled plastic containers in your kitchen. One jar has a sticker 'Sugar', another says 'Salt'. The sticker name is the variable name, and whatever you pour inside is the value. You can change what's inside anytime!
partC_hinglish: Variable ek memory box (dabba) jaisa hota hai jisme hum apna data store karte hain. Jaise marks = 80. Yahan 'marks' variable ka naam hai aur '80' uski value hai. Python mein aapko pehle se batane ki zaroorat nahi hoti ki dabba integer ka hai ya string ka; aap jo value dalenge, Python automatic samajh jayega. User se value lene ke liye hum input() function use karte hain.
partD_examDef: A variable is a symbolic name that refers to a specific memory location holding a data value. In Python, variables are dynamically created upon value assignment using the assignment operator (=).
partE_points: No Explicit Declaration Needed: Unlike C/C++ (e.g., int x;), Python creates a variable automatically the moment you assign a value (e.g., x = 10).
Dynamic Typing: The same variable can hold an integer first, and later hold a string.
Assignment Operator (=): Used to assign the value on the right-hand side to the variable name on the left-hand side.
Multiple Assignment: Python allows a = b = c = 50 or x, y = 10, 20 in a single line.
Reading User Input: input() function reads input from the user. IMPORTANT: input() ALWAYS returns data as a STRING! To get a number, we must typecast it using int() or float().
Naming Restrictions: Same as identifier rules (must begin with a letter or _, no spaces, no special symbols, no keywords).
partF_syntax:
# Variable Assignment
variable_name = value

# Reading String Input
name = input("Enter your name: ")

# Reading Integer Input (Typecasting)
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
partG_example:
# Program to take student input and calculate total marks
name = "Simran"
maths = 40
python = 48

total = maths + python
print("Student Name:", name)
print("Total Marks:", total)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: name = "Simran" creates variable 'name' with string value "Simran".
Line 2: maths = 40 creates variable 'maths' holding integer 40.
Line 3: python = 48 creates variable 'python' holding integer 48.
Line 4: total = maths + python adds 40 and 48, storing 88 in 'total'.
Lines 5-6: print() displays the results.
partJ_output:
Student Name: Simran
Total Marks: 88
partK_mistakes: Forgetting to typecast input(): e.g., age = input() gives string. If user enters 10 and you do age + 5, Python throws TypeError: can only concatenate str to str.
Writing value on left side: 10 = x is ILLEGAL. Variable name must always be on the left side of '='.
Using spaces in variable names: total marks = 100 causes SyntaxError.

oneMark.q: What is the return type of Python's input() function by default?
Can a variable hold different data types at different times in Python?
oneMark.a: Yes, because Python is dynamically typed.

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: How do you read an integer from the user in Python?
Ans: Using int(input("prompt")). The input() function reads the input as a string, and int() converts (typecasts) it into an integer.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is a variable? Explain variable initialization, assignment, naming restrictions, and how user input is read and typecasted in Python with examples.

partM_revision: Variable = named memory box. '=' assigns values. No data type declaration needed. input() always gives string; wrap in int() or float() for numbers.

title: Implicit Declaration & Dynamic Typing
partA_intro: In programming, declaring a variable means telling the computer what type of data it will store. Python uses 'Implicit Declaration', meaning you do not have to specify the type manually; Python determines it automatically based on the assigned value.
partB_realLife: Imagine walking into a shoe store. If you hand the shopkeeper a coin, he knows it's money. If you hand him a coupon, he knows it's a coupon. You don't have to shout 'This is a coin!' before handing it over. He implicitly knows by seeing the object.
partC_hinglish: C ya Java mein agar hume koi number store karna hota tha, toh hume pehle 'int x = 10;' likhna padta tha. Lekin Python itna smart hai ki agar aap sirf 'x = 10' likhenge, toh Python khud samajh jayega ki x integer hai. Ise 'Implicit Declaration' aur 'Dynamic Typing' kehte hain. type() function se hum kisi bhi variable ka type check kar sakte hain.
partD_examDef: Implicit declaration is a feature of Python where variable data types are automatically determined by the interpreter at runtime based on the assigned value, without any explicit type declaration keywords.
partE_points: Dynamic Typing: Variables are not bound to a fixed data type; their type changes dynamically if a new value of another type is assigned.
No Type Keywords: Python does not use 'int x;', 'float y;', etc.
type() Function: Built-in function used to inspect the data type of any variable or value.
Memory Efficiency: Python handles memory allocation and garbage collection automatically.
partF_syntax:
# Checking data type:
type(variable_name)
partG_example:
# Demonstration of Implicit Declaration and Dynamic Typing
val = 100
print(type(val))  # Integer

val = "Now I am a string"
print(type(val))  # String dynamically changed
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: val = 100 assigns integer 100 to val. Python implicitly types val as int.
Line 2: print(type(val)) prints <class 'int'>.
Line 4: val = "Now I am a string" reassigns a string to the same variable val.
Line 5: print(type(val)) prints <class 'str'>, showing dynamic typing in action.
partJ_output:
<class 'int'>
<class 'str'>
partK_mistakes: Writing 'int x = 10'. In Python, this will throw a SyntaxError because 'int' is a type constructor, not a declaration keyword.
Assuming a variable is locked to one type forever. In Python, variable types are fully dynamic.

oneMark.q: Which function is used to find the data type of a variable in Python?
What is meant by dynamic typing in Python?
oneMark.a: Variables can hold values of different data types during execution without explicit declaration.

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Differentiate between static typing and dynamic typing.
Ans: In static typing (like C/Java), variable types must be declared explicitly before use and cannot change. In dynamic typing (Python), types are inferred automatically at runtime and can change dynamically.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Explain the concept of implicit declaration and dynamic typing in Python with suitable program examples and comparison with traditional languages.

partM_revision: Implicit declaration = Python detects type automatically. Dynamic typing = variable type can change at runtime. Use type(x) to inspect type.

title: Number Data Types: int, float, complex
partA_intro: Numbers are fundamental data types in Python used to perform mathematical calculations. Python provides three core numeric types: int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), and complex (numbers with real and imaginary parts).
partB_realLife:
1. int: Counting students in a classroom (e.g., 45 students, cannot be 45.5).
2. float: Weighing flour or sugar (e.g., 2.75 kg).
3. complex: Advanced electrical engineering calculations involving AC current alternating phases.
partC_hinglish:
Python mein numbers 3 tarah ke hote hain:
1. int: Bina point wale poore number, jaise 10, -5, 1000. Python 3 mein int ki koi size limit nahi hoti!
2. float: Point (decimal) wale number, jaise 3.14, 99.9, -0.5.
3. complex: Jisme ek real part hota hai aur ek imaginary part jisme 'j' lagta hai, jaise 3 + 4j. Exam ke liye dhyan rakhe ki Python mein 'i' nahi, 'j' use hota hai!
partD_examDef: Python supports three built-in numeric data types: int for arbitrarily large integers, float for double-precision floating-point numbers, and complex for numbers having a real and imaginary part (represented as a + bj).
partE_points: int: Whole numbers (positive, negative, zero) with unlimited precision in Python 3.
float: Fractional or decimal numbers represented with 64-bit IEEE 754 precision.
complex: Numbers represented as a + bj, where a is real part and b is imaginary part. Python uses 'j' or 'J' for the imaginary unit (NOT 'i').
Accessing complex components: num.real gives the real part, and num.imag gives the imaginary part (both as floats).
partF_syntax:
a = 15          # int
b = 12.75       # float
c = 4 + 3j      # complex
partG_example:
# Program illustrating int, float, and complex numbers
x = 25
y = 14.5
z = 2 + 5j

print("Value of x:", x, "Type:", type(x))
print("Value of y:", y, "Type:", type(y))
print("Value of z:", z, "Type:", type(z))
print("Real part of z:", z.real)
print("Imaginary part of z:", z.imag)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: x = 25 stores an integer.
Line 2: y = 14.5 stores a floating-point number.
Line 3: z = 2 + 5j stores a complex number with real=2 and imaginary=5.
Lines 4-6: Prints values and verified types using type().
Lines 7-8: z.real extracts 2.0 and z.imag extracts 5.0.
partJ_output:
Value of x: 25 Type: <class 'int'>
Value of y: 14.5 Type: <class 'float'>
Value of z: (2+5j) Type: <class 'complex'>
Real part of z: 2.0
Imaginary part of z: 5.0
partK_mistakes: Using 'i' for complex numbers: 3 + 4i causes SyntaxError. In Python, you must use 'j' (e.g., 3 + 4j).
Writing 4j as 4 * j without defining j: Always write the number directly attached to j, e.g., 5j.

oneMark.q: Which symbol represents the imaginary component of a complex number in Python?
What is the data type of the expression 5 / 2 in Python 3?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Explain the numeric data types available in Python with examples.
Ans: 1. int (e.g., 100), 2. float (e.g., 45.8), 3. complex (e.g., 3 + 4j where .real=3.0 and .imag=4.0).
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Describe in detail the numeric data types supported by Python. Explain int, float, and complex numbers with their properties, attributes, and practical examples.

partM_revision: int = whole numbers, float = decimals, complex = real + imaginary with 'j' (e.g. 2 + 3j). Attributes: .real and .imag.

title: Strings (Creation, Indexing & Immutability)
partA_intro: A String is an ordered sequence of characters enclosed within quotation marks. It is used to store text such as words, sentences, roll numbers, or addresses.
partB_realLife: Think of a pearl necklace where each pearl represents a letter. You can point to the first pearl (index 0), second pearl (index 1), or the last pearl (index -1). But you cannot swap a pearl without making a whole new necklace (Strings are immutable).
partC_hinglish: String ka matlab hota hai text (akshar ya shabd). Python mein string ko single quote ('...') ya double quote ("...") mein likhte hain. String ke har character ka ek number hota hai jise 'Index' kehte hain. Index hamesha 0 se start hota hai. Python mein 'Negative Indexing' bhi hoti hai jisme -1 ka matlab aakhiri character hota hai. Ek important exam point: Strings 'Immutable' hoti hain, yaani ek baar banne ke baad unka koi character badla nahi ja sakta.
partD_examDef: A string in Python is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters enclosed in single quotes (' '), double quotes (" "), or triple quotes (''' ''').
partE_points: Creation: s = 'Hello' or s = "Hello" or s = """Hello""".
Positive Indexing: Starts from 0 (left-to-right, 0, 1, 2, ...).
Negative Indexing: Starts from -1 (right-to-left, -1, -2, -3, ...).
Immutability: You cannot change individual characters in a string. s[0] = 'M' will raise a TypeError.
String Length: len(s) returns the total number of characters in the string.
partF_syntax:
s = "Python"
first_char = s[0]    # 'P'
last_char = s[-1]    # 'n'
length = len(s)      # 6
partG_example:
# Program demonstrating string indexing and immutability
subject = "PYTHON"

print("Original String:", subject)
print("First character (index 0):", subject[0])
print("Third character (index 2):", subject[2])
print("Last character (index -1):", subject[-1])
print("Total length:", len(subject))
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: subject = "PYTHON" stores 6 characters: P(0), Y(1), T(2), H(3), O(4), N(5).
Line 3: prints the full string.
Line 4: subject[0] accesses the 0th index ('P').
Line 5: subject[2] accesses the 2nd index ('T').
Line 6: subject[-1] accesses the rightmost character ('N').
Line 7: len(subject) calculates count of characters, which is 6.
partJ_output:
Original String: PYTHON
First character (index 0): P
Third character (index 2): T
Last character (index -1): N
Total length: 6
partK_mistakes: Attempting to modify a string: subject[0] = 'J' throws TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment.
Index out of range: For a string of length 6, accessing subject[6] throws IndexError because valid indices are 0 to 5.

oneMark.q: Are Python strings mutable or immutable?
What is the index of the last character in any non-empty Python string?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: What is negative indexing in Python strings? Explain with an example.
Ans: Negative indexing counts characters from right to left, starting at -1 for the last character, -2 for second-to-last, etc. Example: s = 'EXAM', s[-1] is 'M'.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is a String in Python? Explain string creation, positive and negative indexing, immutability, and built-in string functions with detailed examples.

partM_revision: Strings = sequence of characters. Immutable (cannot change in-place). Left-to-right index begins at 0; Right-to-left index begins at -1. len(s) gives total characters.

title: Boolean Data Type (True / False)
partA_intro: The Boolean data type represents one of two possible values: True or False. It is predominantly used in conditional statements, decision making, and logical evaluations.
partB_realLife: Think of a light switch on a wall. It can only be in one of two states: ON (True) or OFF (False). There is no third state. Similarly, an exam question is either correct or incorrect.
partC_hinglish: Boolean data type mein sirf 2 hi values ho sakti hain: True (sach/haan) ya False (jhooth/naa). Jab bhi hum do numbers ki tulna (comparison) karte hain, jaise 10 > 5, toh Python answer deta hai 'True'. Agar 5 > 10 poochenge toh answer aayega 'False'. Yaad rakhein: True aur False ka 'T' aur 'F' hamesha Capital hota hai!
partD_examDef: Boolean (bool) is a built-in Python data type that can take one of two truth values: True or False. In Python, bool is a subclass of int, where True is equal to 1 and False is equal to 0.
partE_points: Keywords: True and False are reserved keywords in Python.
Capitalization Rule: Must be capitalized (True, False). Writing 'true' or 'false' will result in NameError.
Numeric Equivalence: In arithmetic operations, True acts as 1 and False acts as 0. (e.g., True + True = 2).
bool() Function: Evaluates truth value of any object. Numbers other than 0 are True; 0, empty string "", empty list [] evaluate to False.
partF_syntax:
is_passed = True
is_failed = False
result = 10 > 5  # Evaluates to True
partG_example:
# Program to demonstrate Boolean values and evaluation
is_student = True
marks = 72
is_passed = marks >= 35

print("Is Student:", is_student)
print("Passed Exam:", is_passed)
print("Boolean as integer (True + 5):", True + 5)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: is_student is assigned boolean literal True.
Line 2: marks is set to 72.
Line 3: marks >= 35 checks if 72 is greater than or equal to 35, evaluating to True.
Lines 4-5: Prints boolean values.
Line 6: True + 5 treats True as 1, so 1 + 5 = 6.
partJ_output:
Is Student: True
Passed Exam: True
Boolean as integer (True + 5): 6
partK_mistakes: Writing true or false with lowercase: x = true causes NameError: name 'true' is not defined.
Wrapping True in quotes: x = "True" creates a String (str), NOT a Boolean!

oneMark.q: What is the numeric value of True and False in Python?
What will be the output of bool(0) and bool(10)?
oneMark.a: bool(0) is False; bool(10) is True.

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Explain the Boolean data type in Python with its integer relation.
Ans: The bool data type has two values: True and False. Both are keywords. Internally, True is represented as 1 and False as 0, allowing them to be used in arithmetic operations.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What are basic data types in Python? Explain Numbers, Strings, and Booleans with examples, syntax, memory characteristics, and type conversion.

partM_revision: Boolean has only 2 values: True and False (first letter capital). True == 1, False == 0. bool(0) is False, bool(any_number) is True.

title: Arithmetic Operators (+, -, *, /, //, %, **)
partA_intro: Arithmetic operators are used to perform common mathematical operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division, modulus, and exponentiation.
partB_realLife: Think of a standard pocket calculator. When you press '+' to add prices or '×' to calculate total cost, you are using arithmetic operators.
partC_hinglish:
Arithmetic operators ka use basic maths karne ke liye hota hai. Python mein regular operators (+, -, *) ke alawa 3 bahut important special operators hote hain jo exam mein zaroor aate hain:
1. / (Division): Hamesha float (decimal) answer deta hai (10 / 2 = 5.0).
2. // (Floor Division): Point ke baad ki value ko hata deta hai (10 // 3 = 3).
3. % (Modulus): Bhaag karne ke baad bacha hua 'Remainder' (sheshphal) deta hai (10 % 3 = 1).
4. ** (Exponent/Power): Power nikalne ke liye (2 ** 3 = 8).
partD_examDef: Arithmetic operators are binary operators used to perform standard arithmetic computations between two numeric operands in Python.
partE_points: + (Addition): Adds two values (e.g., 5 + 3 = 8). Also concatenates strings.
- (Subtraction): Subtracts right operand from left operand (e.g., 10 - 4 = 6).
* (Multiplication): Multiplies numbers (e.g., 4 * 3 = 12). Also repeats strings.
/ (Float Division): Always returns a float result (e.g., 7 / 2 = 3.5).
// (Floor Division): Returns the integer quotient rounded down towards minus infinity (e.g., 7 // 2 = 3).
% (Modulus / Remainder): Returns the remainder of division (e.g., 7 % 2 = 1).
** (Exponentiation / Power): Raises left operand to power of right operand (e.g., 2 ** 4 = 16).
partF_syntax:
a = 15
b = 4
add = a + b
floor_div = a // b
rem = a % b
power = 2 ** 3
partG_example:
# Program demonstrating all 7 arithmetic operators
a = 17
b = 5

print("Addition (a + b):", a + b)
print("Subtraction (a - b):", a - b)
print("Multiplication (a * b):", a * b)
print("Float Division (a / b):", a / b)
print("Floor Division (a // b):", a // b)
print("Modulus/Remainder (a % b):", a % b)
print("Exponentiation (2 ** 3):", 2 ** 3)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1-2: a is 17 and b is 5.
Line 4: 17 + 5 evaluates to 22.
Line 5: 17 - 5 evaluates to 12.
Line 6: 17 * 5 evaluates to 85.
Line 7: 17 / 5 evaluates to 3.4 (always float).
Line 8: 17 // 5 evaluates to 3 (drops decimal).
Line 9: 17 % 5 evaluates to 2 (17 = 5 * 3 + 2).
Line 10: 2 ** 3 calculates 2 cubed = 8.
partJ_output:
Addition (a + b): 22
Subtraction (a - b): 12
Multiplication (a * b): 85
Float Division (a / b): 3.4
Floor Division (a // b): 3
Modulus/Remainder (a % b): 2
Exponentiation (2 ** 3): 8
partK_mistakes: Confusing / and //: 10 / 2 returns 5.0 (float), whereas 10 // 2 returns 5 (int).
Division by zero: 10 / 0 or 10 % 0 causes ZeroDivisionError.

oneMark.q: What is the difference between '/' and '//' operators in Python?
oneMark.a: '/' returns float quotient (e.g. 5/2 = 2.5); '//' returns integer floor quotient (5//2 = 2).

oneMark.q: What will be the output of 7 % 3 and 2 ** 3?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Explain the modulus (%) and exponentiation (**) operators with examples.
Ans: Modulus (%) returns remainder: 14 % 4 = 2. Exponentiation (**) raises base to power: 3 ** 2 = 9.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What are Arithmetic operators in Python? Explain each operator with purpose, syntax, examples, dry run, and difference between division and floor division.

partM_revision: +, -, *, / (gives float), // (floor/int quotient), % (remainder), ** (power). Zero division raises ZeroDivisionError.

title: Comparison / Relational Operators (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=)
partA_intro: Comparison or relational operators are used to compare the values of two operands. The result of a comparison is always a Boolean value: either True or False.
partB_realLife: Think of a security guard checking heights at a rollercoaster ride. If height >= 4.5 feet, you can enter; otherwise you cannot. He compares your height against the cutoff.
partC_hinglish: Relational operators do values ki tulna karne ke kaam aate hain. Inka jawab hamesha sirf 'True' ya 'False' mein aata hai. Sabse zaroori baat: Python mein Barabar (Equal to) check karne ke liye double equal to '==' lagaya jata hai, single '=' nahi! Single '=' value assign karta hai, aur '==' value compare karta hai.
partD_examDef: Comparison (relational) operators compare the values of two operands and evaluate to a Boolean truth value (True or False) based on whether the condition holds.
partE_points: == (Equal to): Returns True if both operands are equal (e.g., 5 == 5 is True).
!= (Not Equal to): Returns True if operands are NOT equal (e.g., 5 != 3 is True).
> (Greater than): Returns True if left operand is strictly greater than right operand.
< (Less than): Returns True if left operand is strictly less than right operand.
>= (Greater than or equal to): Returns True if left operand is greater than or equal to right operand.
<= (Less than or equal to): Returns True if left operand is less than or equal to right operand.
Exam Trap: = is assignment, while == is comparison!
partF_syntax:
a == b
a != b
a > b
a <= b
partG_example:
# Program demonstrating comparison operators
x = 20
y = 15

print("x == y:", x == y)   # False
print("x != y:", x != y)   # True
print("x > y:", x > y)     # True
print("x < y:", x < y)     # False
print("x >= 20:", x >= 20) # True
print("y <= 10:", y <= 10) # False
partH_lineByLine: Line 1-2: x is 20, y is 15.
Line 4: 20 == 15 is False.
Line 5: 20 != 15 is True.
Line 6: 20 > 15 is True.
Line 7: 20 < 15 is False.
Line 8: 20 >= 20 is True (since 20 equals 20).
Line 9: 15 <= 10 is False.
partJ_output:
x == y: False
x != y: True
x > y: True
x < y: False
x >= 20: True
y <= 10: False
partK_mistakes: Using single '=' in conditions: if x = 10: causes SyntaxError. You must write if x == 10:.
Writing =< or =>: Invalid syntax! Always put the angle bracket first (<=, >=).

oneMark.q: What is the difference between '=' and '==' in Python?
oneMark.a: '=' is the assignment operator; '==' is the relational comparison operator.

oneMark.q: What will be the output of: 10 >= 10?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: List all comparison operators in Python and their return type.
Ans: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=. Their return type is always Boolean (True or False).
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Explain relational/comparison operators in Python. Differentiate between assignment and comparison with code examples, truth tables, and common errors.

partM_revision: Comparison operators return True or False. == (equal), != (not equal), >, <, >=, <=. Never write = inside condition checks.

title: Increment / Assignment Operators (=, +=, -=, etc.)
partA_intro: Assignment operators are used to store values into variables. Compound (augmented) assignment operators perform an arithmetic operation and assign the result in a single step.
partB_realLife: Think of your piggy bank. If you already have ₹50 and add ₹20 more, you do: Total = Total + 20. In Python shorthand, you simply write: Total += 20.
partC_hinglish: Python mein value store karne ke liye '=' use hota hai. Agar hume kisi variable ki purani value mein hi kuch jodna ya ghatana ho, toh hum short-cut (Compound Assignment) use karte hain. Jaise 'x = x + 5' ko hum 'x += 5' likh sakte hain. Ek zaroori exam point: Python mein C/C++ ki tarah '++' ya '--' operator NAHI hota hai! Python mein increment karne ke liye sirf '+= 1' likhte hain.
partD_examDef: Assignment operators store values into variables. Compound assignment operators (e.g., +=, -=, *=, /=) combine an arithmetic operation with assignment into a single shorthand expression.
partE_points: = (Simple Assignment): Assigns right value to left variable (x = 10).
+= (Add and Assign): x += 5 is equivalent to x = x + 5.
-= (Subtract and Assign): x -= 3 is equivalent to x = x - 3.
*= (Multiply and Assign): x *= 2 is equivalent to x = x * 2.
/= (Divide and Assign): x /= 4 is equivalent to x = x / 4.
//=: Floor divide and assign.
%=: Modulus and assign.
**=: Power and assign.
IMPORTANT EXAM FACT: Python does NOT have pre/post increment operators (x++ or ++x do not exist in Python!).
partF_syntax:
x = 10
x += 5   # x is now 15
x *= 2   # x is now 30
partG_example:
# Program demonstrating compound assignment operators
a = 20
print("Initial value of a:", a)

a += 10  # a = a + 10
print("After a += 10:", a)

a -= 5   # a = a - 5
print("After a -= 5:", a)

a *= 2   # a = a * 2
print("After a *= 2:", a)

a //= 4  # a = a // 4
print("After a //= 4:", a)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: a is initialized to 20.
Line 4: a += 10 adds 10 to 20, making a = 30.
Line 7: a -= 5 subtracts 5 from 30, making a = 25.
Line 10: a *= 2 multiplies 25 by 2, making a = 50.
Line 13: a //= 4 divides 50 by 4, dropping decimals, making a = 12.
partJ_output:
Initial value of a: 20
After a += 10: 30
After a -= 5: 25
After a *= 2: 50
After a //= 4: 12
partK_mistakes: Attempting to use x++: In Python, x++ gives SyntaxError. You must write x += 1.
Writing =+ instead of +=: a =+ 5 assigns positive 5 to a, it does NOT increment!

oneMark.q: Does Python support the '++' increment operator?
oneMark.a: No, Python does not support '++'. We use '+= 1' instead.

oneMark.q: What is the equivalent expression for: x %= 4?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: What are compound assignment operators? Give two examples.
Ans: Compound operators combine arithmetic and assignment into one step. Examples: a += b (a = a + b) and a *= b (a = a * b).
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What are assignment and compound assignment operators in Python? Explain each operator with shorthand equivalents, examples, and explain why ++ is not supported in Python.

partM_revision: Assignment: =. Compound: +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=, **=. Python has NO ++ or --. Always use x += 1.

title: Logical Operators (and, or, not)
partA_intro: Logical operators are used to combine multiple conditional expressions or invert the truth value of a condition. They are essential for building complex decision-making logic.
partB_realLife: Think of exam eligibility: To sit in the exam, you need (Admit Card == True) AND (Attendance >= 75). If either is missing, you cannot sit. But for ID proof, you can show (Aadhar Card OR Voter ID).
partC_hinglish:
Logical operators ka use multiple conditions ko ek sath check karne ke liye hota hai. Python mein teen logical operators hote hain:
1. and: Jab dono conditions True hongi, tabhi result True aayega. Agar ek bhi False hui toh result False.
2. or: Agar dono mein se koi bhi EK condition True ho gayi, toh result True aa jayega.
3. not: Ye ulta (reverse) kar deta hai. True ko False aur False ko True bana deta hai.
Dhyan de: Python mein symbols (&&, ||, !) nahi, seedha English words (and, or, not) use hote hain!
partD_examDef: Logical operators in Python are used to perform logical conjunction (and), disjunction (or), and negation (not) on Boolean expressions.
partE_points: and operator: Evaluates to True only if BOTH operands/conditions are True.
or operator: Evaluates to True if AT LEAST ONE operand/condition is True.
not operator: Unary operator that inverts the Boolean truth value (not True is False).
English words: Python uses lowercase words: 'and', 'or', 'not' (NOT &&, ||, !).
Short-Circuit Evaluation: In 'A and B', if A is False, B is not evaluated. In 'A or B', if A is True, B is not evaluated.
partF_syntax:
condition1 and condition2
condition1 or condition2
not condition
partG_example:
# Program demonstrating logical operators
age = 22
has_license = True

can_drive = (age >= 18) and has_license
print("Can Drive (and):", can_drive)

has_cash = False
has_upi = True
can_pay = has_cash or has_upi
print("Can Pay (or):", can_pay)

print("Negation of True (not True):", not True)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1-2: age is 22, has_license is True.
Line 4: age >= 18 is True, and has_license is True. True and True evaluates to True.
Line 7-8: has_cash is False, has_upi is True. False or True evaluates to True.
Line 11: not True flips the boolean to False.
partJ_output:
Can Drive (and): True
Can Pay (or): True
Negation of True (not True): False
partK_mistakes: Using && or ||: In Python, using && or || results in SyntaxError. Use 'and' and 'or'.
Confusing and / or behavior when combining conditions.

oneMark.q: What will be the result of: (5 > 2) and (10 < 3)?
oneMark.a: False (since True and False is False).

oneMark.q: What will be the result of: not (10 == 10)?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Draw the truth table for the 'and' and 'or' operators in Python.
Ans: 
and: T and T = T; T and F = F; F and T = F; F and F = F.
or: T or T = T; T or F = T; F or T = T; F or F = F.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Explain logical operators in Python with their complete truth tables, short-circuit evaluation mechanism, and practical programming examples.

partM_revision: and = True only if all are True. or = True if any one is True. not = reverses the value. Use words: and, or, not.

title: Identity Operators (is, is not)
partA_intro: Identity operators compare the identity of two objects, verifying whether both variables reference the exact same object in Python's memory space. In contrast, equality operators compare whether the values held by two objects are identical.
partB_realLife: Suppose you and your friend both have the exact same book (same title, same pages, same price). Their contents are equal (==), but they are two separate physical copies in reality. If you both share one single book, then the book has the same identity ('is').
partC_hinglish: Ye exam ka ek favourite question hai! '==' operator do variables ki VALUE (andar ki cheez) check karta hai ki kya dono barabar hain. Jabki 'is' operator check karta hai OBJECT IDENTITY—yaani kya dono variables EK HI OBJECT ko point kar rahe hain. id() function Python mein har object ka ek unique integer identity number return karta hai. Exam mein ise universal physical memory address kehne ke bajaye 'unique object identity integer' kehna technically zyada accurate hai.
partD_examDef: Identity operators ('is' and 'is not') test whether two identifiers refer to the exact same object in Python. The equality operator ('==') tests value equality, whereas 'is' tests object identity equivalence (evaluating id(a) == id(b)).
partE_points: 'is' Operator: Returns True if both variables point to the identical object in memory (id(a) == id(b)).
'is not' Operator: Returns True if both variables point to distinct objects (id(a) != id(b)).
id() Function: Returns an integer representing the unique identity of the object, guaranteed unique and constant for its lifetime.
Equality (==) vs Identity (is): Two distinct list objects can have identical values (== evaluates to True) while having different identities ('is' evaluates to False).
partF_syntax:
x is y
x is not y
partG_example:
# Program demonstrating difference between '==' and 'is'
list1 = [1, 2, 3]
list2 = [1, 2, 3]
list3 = list1

print("list1 == list2:", list1 == list2)     # True (same values)
print("list1 is list2:", list1 is list2)     # False (different objects in memory)
print("list1 is list3:", list1 is list3)     # True (both point to same memory)
print("list1 is not list2:", list1 is not list2) # True
partH_lineByLine: Line 1-2: list1 and list2 are created separately. Both have contents [1, 2, 3] but reside at different memory addresses.
Line 3: list3 = list1 makes list3 refer directly to the existing list1 memory address.
Line 5: list1 == list2 is True because contents are identical.
Line 6: list1 is list2 is False because id(list1) != id(list2).
Line 7: list1 is list3 is True because both point to the same memory location.
partJ_output:
list1 == list2: True
list1 is list2: False
list1 is list3: True
list1 is not list2: True
partK_mistakes: Assuming 'is' and '==' are identical. They are fundamentally different!
Using 'is' to compare numbers or user input strings. Use '==' for value equality.

oneMark.q: What is the difference between '==' and 'is' operator in Python?
oneMark.a: '==' checks for value equality; 'is' checks whether two variables refer to the same object in memory.

oneMark.q: Which built-in function returns the memory address of an object?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Explain identity operators with an example.
Ans: The identity operators are 'is' and 'is not'. They compare memory addresses: 'a is b' returns True if id(a) == id(b). Example: [1,2] is [1,2] evaluates to False.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What are Identity Operators in Python? Distinguish between identity and equality with diagrams, the role of id() function, and Python code examples.

partM_revision: '==' compares values. 'is' compares object identity (id(a) == id(b)). id() returns the unique object identity integer.

title: Operator Precedence & Associativity
partA_intro: When a single mathematical expression contains multiple operators (e.g., 10 + 2 * 3), operator precedence determines which operation is evaluated first. Associativity decides the order of evaluation when operators have the same precedence.
partB_realLife: Think of the BODMAS rule taught in school maths. Brackets are solved first, then Division, Multiplication, Addition, and Subtraction. Python follows a similar strict priority list.
partC_hinglish: Agar ek hi line mein plus, minus, multiply sab aa jaye, toh pehle kaun solve hoga? Ise 'Operator Precedence' kehte hain. Jaise '10 + 2 * 3' mein pehle 2 * 3 = 6 hoga, fir 10 + 6 = 16 banega (na ki 12 * 3 = 36). Python mein sabse zyada priority Parentheses (brackets) ki hoti hai. Jab do operators ki priority barabar hoti hai, toh unhe Left-to-Right solve karte hain (lekin Exponentiation ** Right-to-Left solve hota hai!).
partD_examDef: Operator precedence determines the order in which operators are evaluated in a compound expression. Operator associativity defines the direction (Left-to-Right or Right-to-Left) of evaluation when operators share equal precedence.
partE_points: 1. Parentheses (): Highest precedence of all. Always evaluated first.
2. Exponentiation **: Second highest, evaluated Right-to-Left (e.g., 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 2 ** 9 = 512).
3. Unary operators: +x, -x, ~x.
4. Multiplication, Division, Floor Div, Modulus: *, /, //, % (Left-to-Right).
5. Addition and Subtraction: +, - (Left-to-Right).
6. Comparison operators: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=, is, in.
7. Logical not.
8. Logical and.
9. Logical or: Lowest precedence among logical operators.
10. Assignment operators: =, +=, -=, etc. (Evaluated last, Right-to-Left).
partF_syntax:
# Changing precedence using parentheses:
result1 = 10 + 5 * 2    # 20
result2 = (10 + 5) * 2  # 30
partG_example:
# Program demonstrating operator precedence
val1 = 10 + 2 * 5
val2 = (10 + 2) * 5
val3 = 2 ** 3 ** 2  # Evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9
val4 = 10 > 5 and 3 < 1 or 4 == 4

print("10 + 2 * 5 =", val1)
print("(10 + 2) * 5 =", val2)
print("2 ** 3 ** 2 =", val3)
print("Logical evaluation =", val4)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: * has higher precedence than +, so 2 * 5 = 10, then 10 + 10 = 20.
Line 2: Parentheses () have highest precedence, so (10 + 2) = 12, then 12 * 5 = 60.
Line 3: ** is right-associative, so 3 ** 2 = 9 first, then 2 ** 9 = 512.
Line 4: Comparison first, then 'and', then 'or'. Result evaluates to True.
partK_mistakes: Assuming Left-to-Right for **: Calculating (2 ** 3) ** 2 = 64 instead of 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 512.
Forgetting that 'and' has higher precedence than 'or'.

oneMark.q: Which operator has the highest precedence in Python?
What is the associativity of the exponentiation (**) operator?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Evaluate the expression: 5 + 3 * 2 ** 2.
Ans: 1. 2 ** 2 = 4 (power first), 2. 3 * 4 = 12 (multiply next), 3. 5 + 12 = 17 (addition last). Result = 17.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is operator precedence and associativity? Provide a complete hierarchy table of Python operators and evaluate three complex sample expressions step-by-step.

partM_revision: Precedence: () > ** > *, /, //, % > +, - > comparisons > not > and > or > assignment. ** is right-associative; most others are left-associative.

title: Control Flow & Decision Making Concept
partA_intro: Control flow refers to the order in which individual statements or instructions in a program are executed. By default, programs execute sequentially line-by-line. Decision making (branching) allows a program to choose different paths of execution based on whether a condition is True or False.
partB_realLife: Imagine arriving at a road intersection. If the traffic light is GREEN, you drive forward. If the traffic light is RED, you stop. Your physical action depends on evaluating the real-world condition.
partC_hinglish: Normal code mein computer line 1, line 2, line 3 karke ek ke baad ek chalta hai (Sequential Flow). Lekin aisi situations hoti hain jahan hum chahte hain ki agar koi shart (condition) poori ho, tabhi koi line chale, warna skip ho jaye. Ise 'Decision Making' ya 'Control Flow' kehte hain. Python mein decision making ke liye 'Indentation' (spaces) ka sabse bada role hota hai.
partD_examDef: Control flow defines the sequential or conditional order in which programming statements are evaluated. Decision making statements alter this default linear execution by evaluating conditional Boolean expressions.
partE_points: Sequential Flow: Default top-to-bottom line execution.
Conditional Flow: Executing blocks of code only if a specific condition evaluates to True.
Python Indentation: Unlike C/C++/Java that use curly braces '{ }', Python uses whitespace INDENTATION (typically 4 spaces) to define code blocks.
Colon (:) Requirement: Every conditional header (if, else, elif) must end with a colon (:).
partF_syntax:
if condition:
    # Indented block executed when condition is True
    statement_1
    statement_2
partG_example:
# Demonstration of conditional control flow
temp = 38
print("Checking temperature...")
if temp > 30:
    print("It is a hot day!")
print("Check completed.")
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: temp = 38 initializes temperature variable.
Line 2: Prints 'Checking temperature...'.
Line 3: if temp > 30: tests if 38 > 30 (True).
Line 4: Because condition is True, indented line prints 'It is a hot day!'.
Line 5: Unindented line runs regardless of the condition.
partJ_output:
Checking temperature...
It is a hot day!
Check completed.
partK_mistakes: Forgetting colon (:) at end of if statement: if x > 5 causes SyntaxError: expected ':'.
Inconsistent Indentation: Mixing tabs and spaces or not indenting causes IndentationError.

oneMark.q: What character is used in Python to indicate the start of an indented block?
What does Python use instead of curly braces {} to define code blocks?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: What is control flow? Explain the role of indentation in Python.
Ans: Control flow is the execution order of program instructions. Python uses uniform whitespace indentation to delimit blocks of statements following compound statements like if, while, and def.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is control flow and decision making in Python? Explain the significance of indentation, relational conditions, and types of conditional statements with detailed flowcharts and examples.

partM_revision: Control flow = order of execution. Python uses 4-space indentation instead of {}. Always put a colon ':' after if/else/elif headers.

title: Simple if Statement
partA_intro: The simple if statement is the most basic decision-making construct. It executes an indented block of code only if a specified test condition evaluates to True. If the condition is False, the block is bypassed.
partB_realLife: Think of an umbrella rule: IF it is raining outside, open your umbrella. If it is not raining, do nothing and just keep walking.
partC_hinglish: Simple if statement sabse aasan hota hai. Ye kehta hai: 'Agar ye shart sach hai, toh ye kaam karo. Agar sach nahi hai, toh aage badh jao'. Agar condition False ho jati hai, toh if ke andar ka code chalta hi nahi hai aur program normal agli line par chala jata hai.
partD_examDef: The simple if statement evaluates a test expression. If the expression resolves to True, the statements inside the if block are executed; otherwise, they are skipped entirely.
partE_points: Keywords: Uses the reserved keyword 'if'.
Syntax format: if condition: followed by an indented block.
One-way decision: It only specifies what to do when condition is True. It has no alternate branch if condition is False.
Non-zero values in condition evaluate as True; 0 or None evaluate as False.
partG_example:
# Program to check if a student has passing marks
marks = 65

if marks >= 35:
    print("Congratulations!")
    print("You have passed the examination.")

print("Evaluation complete.")
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: marks = 65 initializes the marks variable.
Line 3: if marks >= 35: checks 65 >= 35 (evaluates to True).
Line 4-5: Both indented lines execute because condition is True.
Line 7: Out-of-block print executes sequentially.
partJ_output:
Congratulations!
You have passed the examination.
Evaluation complete.
partK_mistakes: Leaving the if block empty without a pass statement causes IndentationError: expected an indented block.
Putting condition inside unnecessary brackets or forgetting the colon (:).

oneMark.q: What happens in a simple if statement when the condition is False?
oneMark.a: The indented block is skipped and program execution continues with the next statement.

oneMark.q: Is the condition in an if statement required to be enclosed in parentheses in Python?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Write the syntax and draw the flowchart for a simple if statement in Python.
Ans: Syntax: `if condition:` indented statements. Flowchart shows condition box branching to 'True -> Statement Block' and 'False -> Next Statement'.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Explain the simple if statement in Python with syntax, flowchart, dry-run table, and practical program examples.

partM_revision: if condition: runs code only when condition is True. If False, skips it. Indentation is mandatory.

title: if-else Statement
partA_intro: The if-else statement provides a two-way decision branch. It executes one block of code if the test condition is True, and an alternative block of code under 'else' if the condition evaluates to False.
partB_realLife: Think of a coin toss: If it is HEADS, Team A bats. ELSE, Team B bats. Exactly one of the two outcomes will happen; you can never have both or neither.
partC_hinglish: if-else do-tarfa (two-way) decision ke liye hota hai: 'Agar condition sach hai toh if wala dabba chalao, WARNA (else) doosra dabba chalao'. if aur else dono mein se koi EK hi block hamesha chalega, dono kabhi ek sath nahi chal sakte. Exam ke liye note karein: else ke sath koi condition nahi likhi jati, sirf colon (:) lagta hai.
partD_examDef: The if-else statement evaluates a condition and executes the if block when True, or transfers control to the else block when False, ensuring one of two code blocks is always executed.
partE_points: Two-way Branching: Guarantees execution of exactly one block.
Keyword else: Must be written at the exact same indentation level as the corresponding if.
No Condition for else: An else statement does NOT take a condition (e.g., else x < 10: is a SyntaxError).
Colon Required: Both 'if condition:' and 'else:' must end with a colon (:).
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: num = 17 stores 17.
Line 3: num % 2 calculates remainder of 17 / 2, which is 1. 1 == 0 is False.
Line 4: if block is skipped because condition was False.
Line 5: else: is triggered.
Line 6: Executes indented else block: prints '17 is an ODD number'.
partJ_output: 17 is an ODD number
partK_mistakes: Adding condition to else: writing 'else num < 10:' causes SyntaxError. (Use elif if you have a condition!).
Mismatched Indentation: Putting 'else' at a different indentation level than its 'if'.

oneMark.q: Can an 'else' block exist without a preceding 'if' statement?
oneMark.a: No, an 'else' block must always follow an 'if' (or 'elif') statement.

oneMark.q: What will be the output if num = 10 for: if num > 10: print('A') else: print('B')?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Write a Python program using if-else to find whether a student passed or failed (pass marks = 35).
Ans:
marks = int(input())
if marks >= 35:
    print('Pass')
else:
    print('Fail')
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Explain the if-else conditional statement in Python with syntax, flowchart, dry-run, and write a program to check whether a given year is a leap year.

partM_revision: if-else = two-way decision. If condition is True -> if block runs; if False -> else block runs. Never put a condition in else!

title: if-elif-else Ladder
partA_intro: The if-elif-else statement is a multi-way decision branch used when a program needs to test multiple conditions sequentially. 'elif' is Python's short form for 'else if'.
partB_realLife: Think of college grading: If marks >= 75 -> Distinction; Elif marks >= 60 -> First Division; Elif marks >= 50 -> Second Division; Elif marks >= 35 -> Third Division; Else -> Fail.
partC_hinglish: Jab hamare paas sirf do raste nahi, balki 3 ya usse zyada options hote hain (multi-way branching), tab hum 'elif' ladder ka use karte hain. Python mein 'else if' ko chhota karke 'elif' likha jata hai. Interpreter upar se pehli condition check karta hai; jo pehli condition True milti hai, sirf uska code chalata hai aur baaki poori ladder ko chhod kar bahar aa jata hai.
partD_examDef: The if-elif-else ladder evaluates multiple conditional expressions in top-down sequential order. As soon as one condition evaluates to True, its corresponding block executes and the rest of the ladder is bypassed.
partE_points: Keyword elif: Python's unique contraction for 'else if'.
Multi-way Decision: Allows testing as many conditions as needed.
Short-circuit Exit: Only the first matching True block executes; subsequent elif conditions are not even evaluated.
Optional Final else: Catches any cases where none of the if or elif conditions evaluated to True.
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: marks = 82.
Line 3: if marks >= 90: 82 >= 90 is False, moves to next elif.
Line 5: elif marks >= 75: 82 >= 75 is True! grade = 'A' executes.
Lines 7-11: All remaining elif and else blocks are skipped automatically.
Line 13: Prints marks and calculated grade.
partJ_output: Marks: 82 | Grade: A
partK_mistakes: Writing 'else if' instead of 'elif': Python does not recognize 'else if' as two words; you must write 'elif'.
Wrong order of conditions: Testing marks >= 35 before marks >= 75 would make all students get 'C' grade because the first matching condition stops the ladder!

oneMark.q: What is the keyword used in Python for 'else if'?
Can an if-elif ladder have multiple elif blocks?
oneMark.a: Yes, any number of elif blocks can be used.

partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is multi-way branching in Python? Explain the if-elif-else construct with a complete real-world marks-to-grade program, flowchart, and detailed execution dry run.

partM_revision: elif = else if in Python. Evaluates from top to bottom. As soon as one condition is True, executes it and ignores the rest.

title: Nested if Statement
partA_intro: A nested if statement is an if statement placed inside the body of another if (or else) statement. It is used when an action depends on multiple levels of sequential criteria.
partB_realLife: Think of an ATM machine: 1st condition: Is the ATM PIN correct? IF yes, only then 2nd condition is checked: Is Account Balance sufficient? If PIN itself is wrong, balance check never happens.
partC_hinglish: Nested if ka matlab hota hai 'ek if ke pet (body) ke andar doosra if rakhna'. Pehle bahar wala if check hoga. Agar bahar wala if True hoga, tabhi computer andar wale if ko check karega. Agar bahar wala hi False ho gaya, toh andar wale if ka darwaza khulega hi nahi! Isme indentation ka khaas khayal rakhna hota hai.
partD_examDef: A nested if statement occurs when an if, if-else, or if-elif block is placed within the body of another if or else block to evaluate hierarchical conditions.
partE_points: Hierarchical Decisions: Handles multi-level dependent conditions.
Deep Indentation: The inner if block is indented one level further inside the outer if block.
Execution Rule: Inner condition is only tested if the outer condition evaluates to True.
Can nest within both 'if' and 'else' blocks.
partH_lineByLine: Line 1-2: age = 21, weight = 52.
Line 4: if age >= 18: 21 >= 18 is True, so execution enters the outer block.
Line 5: Inner check if weight >= 50: 52 >= 50 is True.
Line 6: Executes inner print: 'Eligible to donate blood.'.
Lines 7-10: Respective inner and outer else blocks are ignored.
partJ_output: Eligible to donate blood.
partK_mistakes: Indentation mismatch: If the inner if is not properly indented, Python treats it as a sequential statement outside the outer if.
Excessive nesting: Nesting too deeply makes code difficult to read (often replaceable with logical 'and' operators).

oneMark.q: What is meant by a 'nested' statement in Python?
oneMark.a: A statement placed inside the body of another statement of the same kind.

oneMark.q: When does the inner if statement execute in a nested if block?
oneMark.a: Only when the outer if condition evaluates to True.

partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is nested if statement? Explain its syntax, indentation hierarchy, and write a complete program to find the greatest among three distinct numbers using nested if.

partM_revision: Nested if = an if inside another if. Inner if only evaluates if outer if is True. Keep indentation consistent.

title: while Loop with Counter & Condition
partA_intro: A loop is used to execute a block of statements repeatedly as long as a specified condition remains True. The while loop is known as an 'entry-controlled loop' because the condition is checked at the very beginning before executing the loop body.
partB_realLife: Think of a tea vendor filling cups: WHILE there are empty cups on the tray, pour tea into the next cup. Stop pouring when there are no empty cups left.
partC_hinglish:
Loop ka matlab hota hai kisi kaam ko baar-baar repeat karna. Agar aapko 1 se 100 tak ginti print karni hai, toh aap 100 baar print() nahi likhenge, balki ek loop chala denge. while loop tab tak chalta rehta hai jab tak uski condition True rehti hai. Isme 3 cheezein zaroori hoti hain:
1. Initialization: Counter kahaan se shuru hoga (i = 1).
2. Condition: Kahaan tak chalega (i <= 10).
3. Increment/Update: Har round ke baad counter kitna badhega (i += 1). Agar update karna bhool gaye toh loop kabhi rukega hi nahi (Infinite Loop ban jayega!).
partD_examDef: A while loop is an entry-controlled iterative control structure in Python that repeatedly executes a target block of statements as long as the governing test condition evaluates to True.
partE_points: Entry-Controlled: Condition is checked at the top before loop execution. If condition is False initially, loop body executes 0 times.
Three Essential Parts: 1. Initialization (i = 1), 2. Condition (while i <= n:), 3. Update/Increment (i += 1).
Infinite Loop Warning: If the condition never becomes False, the loop runs endlessly until memory runs out or user forces termination.
Optional else with while: An else block attached to a while loop executes once when the loop condition becomes False naturally (not via break).
partF_syntax:
counter = initial_value
while condition:
    # Loop body
    statements
    counter += step_value
partG_example:
# Program to print numbers 1 to 5 and their sum using while loop
i = 1
total = 0

while i <= 5:
    print("Current number:", i)
    total += i
    i += 1  # Increment counter

print("Final Sum:", total)
partH_lineByLine: Line 1-2: i is initialized to 1, total to 0.
Line 4: while i <= 5 checks: 1 <= 5 (True).
Line 5-7: Prints 1, adds to total (total=1), increments i to 2.
Loop repeats for i = 2, 3, 4, 5.
When i becomes 6, 6 <= 5 evaluates to False. Loop terminates.
Line 9: Prints final sum (15).
partJ_output:
Current number: 1
Current number: 2
Current number: 3
Current number: 4
Current number: 5
Final Sum: 15
partK_mistakes: Forgetting to increment the loop counter (e.g. leaving out i += 1): Causes an infinite loop that hangs the system.
Off-by-one errors: Writing while i < 5 instead of while i <= 5 stops at 4 instead of 5.

oneMark.q: Why is the while loop called an entry-controlled loop?
oneMark.a: Because its condition is tested at the entry (beginning) before executing the loop body.

oneMark.q: What happens if the condition of a while loop is False at the very start?
oneMark.a: The loop body is not executed even once (0 times).

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: What is an infinite loop? Give an example using while loop.
Ans: An infinite loop never terminates because its condition always remains True. Example: while True: print('Hello').
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is a while loop in Python? Explain its components, syntax, flowchart, dry-run, and write a program to reverse a given integer number (e.g., 1234 -> 4321).

partM_revision: while condition: checks condition before every turn. Requires initialization, condition, and increment (i += 1) to avoid infinite loop.

title: for Loop & Iteration
partA_intro: The for loop in Python is used to iterate over the elements of any sequence (such as a string, list, tuple, or range). It automatically visits each element in order from start to finish without needing manual counter incrementation.
partB_realLife: Think of a postman delivering letters from his bag. He reaches into the bag, takes out letter #1 and delivers it, takes letter #2 and delivers it, and continues until the bag is empty. He doesn't need to manually count; the contents of the bag guide him.
partC_hinglish: C ya Java mein for loop mein teen cheezein likhni padti thi. Lekin Python ka for loop bilkul alag aur bahut aasan hai! Python ka for loop kisi sequence (jaise String, List, ya range) ke har item par ek-ek karke ghoomta hai. Isme aapko alag se 'i += 1' likhne ki zaroorat nahi hoti; Python apne aap agle item par badh jata hai. Isme 'in' keyword ka use hota hai.
partD_examDef: A for loop in Python is a collection-controlled iteration statement that traverses each item in any iterable sequence (such as a list, string, or range) in sequential order.
partE_points: Sequence Traversal: Iterates through lists, strings, tuples, and ranges.
Keyword 'in': Connects the iteration variable to the target sequence.
Automatic Progression: Automatically moves to the next element on each iteration.
No Index Out of Range: Eliminates off-by-one errors commonly associated with manual indexing.
Optional else: Python's for loop can have an 'else' block that runs when the sequence is exhausted.
partG_example:
# Program iterating over a string and a list using for loop
print("Iterating over String:")
for ch in "PY":
    print("Character:", ch)

print("Iterating over List:")
marks = [35, 42, 48]
for m in marks:
    print("Mark:", m)
partH_lineByLine: Line 2: for ch in "PY": assigns 'P' to ch in round 1, then 'Y' in round 2.
Line 3: Prints each character.
Line 6: marks = [35, 42, 48] defines a list of 3 items.
Line 7: for m in marks: sets m = 35, then m = 42, then m = 48.
Line 8: Prints each mark sequentially.
partJ_output:
Iterating over String:
Character: P
Character: Y
Iterating over List:
Mark: 35
Mark: 42
Mark: 48
partK_mistakes: Using a non-iterable with for loop: for i in 10: raises TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable (use range(10) instead).
Modifying a list while iterating over it with a for loop can cause unexpected skipped items.

oneMark.q: Which keyword is used to iterate over a sequence in a for loop?
Can a Python for loop iterate directly over characters in a string?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Differentiate between while loop and for loop in Python.
Ans: while loop is condition-controlled (repeats while condition is True). for loop is collection-controlled (iterates through elements of a sequence/range).
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is a for loop in Python? Explain sequence iteration with strings and lists, comparison with while loop, syntax, dry-run, and write a program to count vowels in a given string.

partM_revision: for item in sequence: automatically visits every element. Works with strings, lists, range(). No manual i += 1 required.

title: range() Function (start, stop, step)
partA_intro: The range() function is a built-in Python function that generates an immutable sequence of integers. It is the most commonly used tool for controlling how many times a for loop runs.
partB_realLife: Think of buying bus tickets numbered 1 to 10. You start at seat 1, finish before seat 11, and advance 1 seat at a time. If you only want odd seats, you step by 2 (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).
partC_hinglish:
range() function numbers ki ek series (ginti) generate karta hai. Isme 3 parameters ho sakte hain: range(start, stop, step).
1. start: Kahaan se shuru karna hai (Default = 0).
2. stop: Kahaan RUKNA hai. SABSE BADA EXAM RULE: range hamesha 'stop - 1' tak hi chalta hai! Agar aapne range(1, 5) likha hai, toh ye 1, 2, 3, 4 tak hi chalega, 5 ko touch nahi karega.
3. step: Kitne ka gap (jump) lena hai (Default = 1). Agar step -1 ho toh ulta (reverse) ginti chalti hai.
partD_examDef: The range() function is a built-in Python type that generates an immutable arithmetic progression of integers defined by three parameters: start, stop (exclusive), and step.
partE_points: 1 Argument: range(stop) -> starts at 0, steps by 1, ends at stop-1. E.g., range(4) generates 0, 1, 2, 3.
2 Arguments: range(start, stop) -> starts at start, ends at stop-1. E.g., range(2, 6) generates 2, 3, 4, 5.
3 Arguments: range(start, stop, step) -> steps by specified increment. E.g., range(1, 10, 2) generates 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
Negative Step: range(5, 0, -1) generates countdown: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
Memory Efficient: Generates numbers on demand (lazy evaluation), saving memory.
partF_syntax:
range(stop)
range(start, stop)
range(start, stop, step)
partG_example:
# Demonstration of 1, 2, and 3 argument forms of range()
print('1-arg range(3):')
for i in range(3):
    print(i, end=' ')
print()  # newline

print('2-arg range(2, 6):')
for i in range(2, 6):
    print(i, end=' ')
print()  # newline

print('3-arg range(10, 0, -2):')
for i in range(10, 0, -2):
    print(i, end=' ')
print()  # newline
partH_lineByLine: Line 2-4: range(3) produces 0, 1, 2 (stop is 3, so ends at 3-1=2).
Line 6-8: range(2, 6) starts at 2 and produces 2, 3, 4, 5.
Line 10-12: range(10, 0, -2) starts at 10, decreases by 2 each round: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2.
partK_mistakes: Expecting range(1, 5) to include 5: Stop value is ALWAYS exclusive (n-1).
Providing step 0: range(1, 5, 0) raises ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero.

oneMark.q: What integers are generated by range(2, 7)?
What is the default start value and step value of range() if omitted?

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Explain the three parameters of the range() function in Python.
Ans: 1. start (inclusive initial value), 2. stop (exclusive upper/lower limit), 3. step (difference between consecutive values).
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: Explain the range() function in Python with all three variations of syntax. Discuss negative stepping, memory advantages, and write a program to calculate the factorial of a number using for loop and range().

partM_revision: range(start, stop, step) generates integer sequences. Stop value is EXCLUDED (runs up to stop-1). Default start = 0, default step = 1.

title: Nested Loops
partA_intro: A nested loop is a loop inside the body of another loop. The 'outer loop' controls the number of complete cycles, and for each single iteration of the outer loop, the 'inner loop' executes completely from start to finish.
partB_realLife: Think of an analog wall clock: For every single hour that passes (outer loop), the minute hand must complete a full 60-minute circle (inner loop).
partC_hinglish: Nested loop ka matlab hota hai 'loop ke andar doosra loop'. Bahar wale loop ko 'Outer Loop' aur andar wale ko 'Inner Loop' kehte hain. Rule ye hai ki jab bahar wala loop 1 baar chalta hai, toh andar wala loop apni poori ginti khatam karta hai. College exam mein 'Pattern printing' (jaise stars * ya numbers ke triangle) ke 14-marks ke question nested loop se hi aate hain!
partD_examDef: A nested loop is a loop structure where one loop (inner loop) is contained entirely inside the body of another loop (outer loop). The inner loop completes all its iterations for each single iteration of the outer loop.
partE_points: Total Iterations: Equal to (Outer loop iterations) * (Inner loop iterations).
Common Use: Matrix operations, multi-dimensional lists, and geometric/star pattern printing.
Indentation Hierarchy: Inner loop must be indented inside the outer loop body.
Any combination: Can nest for inside for, while inside while, or while inside for.
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: rows = 4 sets 4 rows to print.
Line 3: for i in range(1, 5): outer loop runs for i = 1, 2, 3, 4.
Line 4: for j in range(1, i + 1): inner loop runs from 1 to i stars.
Line 5: print("*", end=" ") prints star on the same line.
Line 6: print() drops down to the next row after inner loop finishes.

partI_dryRun.action: Inner loop j runs 1 to 1 -> prints 1 star
Inner loop j runs 1 to 2 -> prints 2 stars
Inner loop j runs 1 to 3 -> prints 3 stars
Inner loop j runs 1 to 4 -> prints 4 stars

partK_mistakes: Using the same loop variable name for both outer and inner loops (e.g. for i in ... inside for i in ... overrides the outer counter).
Forgetting print() at the end of outer loop causing all output to print on one horizontal line.

oneMark.q: If an outer loop runs 3 times and an inner loop runs 4 times, how many total times does the inner loop body execute?
Can a while loop be nested inside a for loop in Python?
oneMark.a: Yes, loops of different types can be freely nested.

partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What is a nested loop in Python? Explain how outer and inner loops synchronize. Write Python programs to print: (a) a number triangle pattern and (b) a multiplication table from 1 to 5.

partM_revision: Nested loop = loop inside a loop. For each 1 step of outer loop, inner loop runs completely. Essential for pattern printing.

title: Branching Statements: break, continue, pass
partA_intro: Branching (jump) statements are used to alter the standard execution flow of loops. Python provides three key jump statements: break (terminates loop), continue (skips to next iteration), and pass (null placeholder).
partB_realLife:
1. break: Emergency brake on a train. When pulled, train stops immediately.
2. continue: Skipping a song in a playlist you dislike to go directly to the next song.
3. pass: An empty cardboard box reserved on a shelf to put items into later.
partC_hinglish:
Exam ke 1-mark aur short notes ke liye ye teen statements SABSE IMPORTANT hain:
1. break: Loop ko TURANT KHATAM kar deta hai aur loop ke bahar fek deta hai.
2. continue: Sirf CURRENT round (iteration) ko wahi chhod deta hai aur TURANT AGLI round par chala jata hai (loop khatam nahi hota, bas wo ek round skip hota hai).
3. pass: Ye ek 'khali' (null) statement hai. Python mein code blocks ko khali nahi chhod sakte warna error aata hai. Agar aapko koi loop ya if baad mein likhna hai, toh aap wahan 'pass' likh dete hain taaki koi error na aaye.
partD_examDef: Branching statements alter loop execution: 'break' terminates the nearest enclosing loop immediately; 'continue' abandons the current iteration and jumps to the next; 'pass' is a null syntactic placeholder that performs no operation.
partE_points: break: Immediately exits the loop, transferring control to the statement directly after the loop block.
continue: Bypasses remaining statements in current loop cycle and advances to the next iteration.
pass: Null statement; executed by interpreter as a NO-OP (no operation). Used to prevent IndentationError on empty blocks.
break and else: When a loop terminates via 'break', its optional 'else' block is NOT executed.
partH_lineByLine: Line 3-6: When i == 3, break executes. Loop immediately terminates. Only 1, 2 are printed.
Line 9-12: When i == 3, continue executes. print(i) is skipped for 3, and loop moves to 4. Prints 1 2 4 5.
Line 15-18: When i == 2, pass runs (does nothing). All 1 2 3 are printed.
partJ_output:
Demonstrating break (stops at 3):
1 2 
Demonstrating continue (skips 3):
1 2 4 5 
Demonstrating pass (placeholder):
1 2 3
partK_mistakes: Confusing break with continue: break KILLS the entire loop; continue only SKIPS the current turn.
Assuming pass skips to the next iteration: pass does NOT skip anything! It simply does nothing and moves to the next line.

oneMark.q: Which statement is used to terminate a loop completely in Python?
What is the purpose of the 'pass' statement in Python?
oneMark.a: It acts as a syntactic placeholder that performs no operation (null statement).

partL_examPrep.shortAnswer:
Q: Distinguish between 'break' and 'continue' statements with examples.
Ans: 'break' terminates loop completely, jumping outside. 'continue' skips remaining lines of current iteration and proceeds to next iteration.
partL_examPrep.fourteenMark: Q: What are jump/branching statements in Python? Explain break, continue, and pass in detail with syntax, flowcharts, difference table, and practical code examples.

partM_revision: break = exit loop immediately. continue = skip current turn and start next turn. pass = empty placeholder (does nothing).

title: Creating Lists & Memory Representation
partA_intro: A list in Python is an ordered, mutable sequence that stores REFERENCES to objects. Unlike primitive arrays in C that store raw data bytes contiguously, a Python list stores a contiguous array of pointers (references) to objects located elsewhere in memory, which allows it to hold heterogeneous (mixed) data types.
partB_realLife: Think of a student's pencil pouch. It contains a pen, pencil, eraser, sharpener, and scale. You can add new stationery, remove an eraser, or replace a blue pen with a black pen anytime.
partC_hinglish: List Python ka sabse popular aur versatile data type hai jise Square Brackets [ ] mein likhte hain. C language ke array mein direct numbers ek ke baad ek raw bytes mein store hote the, isliye sabka ek hi type hona zaroori tha. Lekin Python list asal mein REFERENCES (pointers/addresses) ka array hoti hai! List ke dabbo mein values nahi, balki values ke references store hote hain. Isliye Python list aasaani se number, string, float sab ek sath store kar sakti hai (Heterogeneous collection). Aur ye Mutable hoti hai, yaani elements ko badla ja sakta hai.
partD_examDef: A list is an ordered, mutable collection of object references enclosed in square brackets [ ]. Internally, it is implemented as a dynamic array of pointers to objects, enabling heterogeneous storage and in-place element modification.
partE_points: Stores Object References: Python lists store references (pointers) to objects, not the raw primitive values contiguously in-line.
Heterogeneous: Can hold elements of different data types (e.g., [101, 'Anjali', 82.5, True]) because each slot holds a uniform object reference pointer.
Ordered Sequence: Elements maintain the order of insertion and are accessible via zero-based indexing.
Mutable: Elements can be updated, appended, and deleted in-place.
Dynamic Resizing: Allocates and re-allocates memory automatically as elements are added or removed.
partF_syntax:
empty_list = []
homogeneous_list = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
mixed_list = [101, "Rohan", 78.5, True]
partG_example:
# Program to demonstrate creating various types of lists
empty = []
integers = [10, 20, 30]
student = [101, "Simran", 89.5, True]

print("Empty list:", empty)
print("Integer list:", integers)
print("Heterogeneous list:", student)
print("Type of student:", type(student))
print("Total elements:", len(student))
partH_lineByLine: Line 1: Creates an empty list [].
Line 2: Creates a list of integers.
Line 3: Creates a list containing an int, string, float, and boolean.
Lines 5-7: Displays the lists.
Line 8: type(student) confirms <class 'list'>.
